The accounts differ over exactly how Quṣayy gained control, but they agree that it did not happen without conflict. Fighting took place, and Quṣayy eventually defeated Khuzāʿa, either directly in war or after the dispute was referred for judgment to Yaʿmur ibn ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb of Kināna.
We do not know the exact date of these events.

The chroniclers give us little help except for one clue in a report claiming that Quṣayy bought control of the Kaʿba from Abū Ghubshān al-Khuzāʿī in exchange for a wineskin and a camel. This transaction was said to have given rise to the proverb:
“A worse bargain than the bargain of Abū Ghubshān.”
The same report says that this happened during the reign of al-Mundhir ibn al-Nuʿmān, king of al-Ḥīra.
Even though this detail appears within the legendary story of the “bargain,” it gives us an indirect clue about when Quraysh, represented by Quṣayy, first gained leadership over Mecca.
The al-Mundhir ibn al-Nuʿmān mentioned here must be the son of al-Nuʿmān I ibn Imruʾ al-Qays II.

It cannot be the later al-Mundhir ibn al-Nuʿmān of 631–632, “whom the Arabs called al-Gharūr and who was killed in Bahrain on the day of Jawāthā,” and who ruled al-Ḥīra for only eight months, “until Khālid ibn al-Walīd arrived in al-Ḥīra.” That ruler belonged to the period when Islam had already appeared.
The earlier al-Mundhir succeeded his father al-Nuʿmān I as ruler of al-Ḥīra in AD 418.
From this indirect evidence, we can conclude that Quraysh gained leadership over Mecca during the first half of the fifth century.
In our view, this conclusion is probably correct. It also gives the events and developments of late pre-Islamic Western Arabia a normal historical logic.

The changes associated with the period of Quraysh’s rule in Mecca could hardly have arisen during the very short period immediately before the appearance of Islam, as the reports of the chroniclers might sometimes suggest.
Historical development requires more time than that.

For the same reason, the role played by Quṣayy himself at the beginning of Quraysh’s leadership in Mecca should not really be seen as the beginning of the process. It was more likely the result of a much longer historical development in which Mecca had already played an important role.

The developments that appeared once Quraysh’s leadership was firmly established under Quṣayy represented a qualitative leap—a major change produced by many smaller changes that had already been building over time.
These earlier changes grew out of an increasingly close relationship between two developments.
On one side was the new division of labor taking shape both in settled communities and in the desert.
On the other was the expansion of commercial middlemen and the growing use of money in exchange across the markets of the Arabian Peninsula.
The chroniclers agree that once Quṣayy had secured leadership over Mecca, a number of major changes followed.

They give us many complicated and sometimes inconsistent details. But beneath those details lies historical material that helps us understand both the changes themselves and the direction in which they were moving.
Once we separate the useful evidence from the surrounding details, several main points emerge.
First — The Social Division of Meccan Society
The chroniclers say that when Quṣayy took control of Quraysh in Mecca, he divided Mecca into residential quarters among his people and assigned each group of Quraysh its place.
We do not need to accept the chroniclers’ suggestion that Quṣayy simply decided, by his own personal will, to reorganize the city in this way.
What matters to us is the historical meaning of the event.

We see it as the result of objective historical conditions rather than the decision of one individual. A particular process of development had matured to the point where this change became possible at the right time and in the right place.
To understand its historical meaning, however, we first have to understand what the change actually involved.
In practice, it amounted to a social classification of the inhabitants of Mecca from among the clans of Quraysh and their allies.
One group occupied the central parts of Mecca around the Kaʿba. Because they lived in the biṭāḥ, the low-lying central area, they became known as Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ.
A second, lower-ranking group lived on the outskirts of Mecca and became known as Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir.
But what was this classification based on?
We know that Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir were poor or only partly settled, and that their financial position was weak. Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ, by contrast, included “the merchants and the wealthy.”
So the division was based on financial, economic and social position rather than on tribal custom.
Both groups belonged either to Quraysh itself or to groups allied with Quraysh. One was Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ and the other Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir. Both, in that sense, were part of Quraysh.

If tribal belonging alone had determined the division, all the clans of Quraysh would have occupied the preferred central area, while the allied clans from outside Quraysh would have been placed on the outskirts.
But that was no longer how things worked.
The old tribal values had already begun to weaken, together with the tribal system itself.
A new situation was producing new values. Commercial and social development was placing financial and trading position above older tribal considerations.
This is why Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū ʿAbd al-Dār came to stand at the front of Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ: they had become wealthier and more powerful in trade.

The same standard continued to operate afterward. The Umayyads eventually took the leading position within pre-Islamic Quraysh because they became its richest merchants and extended their financial influence over many tribes of the Hijaz outside Mecca.

If we go back to the beginning of Quraysh’s leadership—that is, to the period of Quṣayy, which the chroniclers treat as its starting point—we find that Ibn al-Kalbī and Ibn Isḥāq give essentially the same explanation for the transfer of power in Mecca from Khuzāʿa to Quraysh.
They say that when Ḥulayl ibn Ḥubshiyya, chief of Khuzāʿa and father of Ḥubbā, Quṣayy’s wife, died, Abū Ghubshān took over the guardianship of the Kaʿba.

By this time, however, “the descendants of Quṣayy had spread, his wealth had increased, and his standing had grown. Quṣayy therefore believed that he had a stronger claim than Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr to the Kaʿba and to authority over Mecca.”

Here, even within the traditional account, we can see that the growth of wealth—and the higher social standing that came with it—was treated as a legitimate basis for Quṣayy’s claim to rule over the Kaʿba and Mecca.
The growing wealth of Quraysh increasingly changed the values of tribal society.

New values emerged in which material and economic position became the main point of reference, even though many tribal considerations still survived and continued to influence public life in a secondary way.
Through this process, Mecca moved to the center of the forces breaking down the old economic and social structure of tribal society.
Engels describes money and usury in Athenian society as forces that brought oppression and loss of freedom to the population.
He also says that no law threw the debtor at the feet of the moneylender more completely than the laws of the ancient Greeks and Romans.
Broadly speaking, this description also applies to what was happening in Mecca and the rest of Western Arabia.

Wealth and money had become heavily concentrated in the hands of the leading men of Quraysh. These men were becoming an aristocracy not only within Mecca but within pre-Islamic society more generally.
As their wealth grew, the gap in wealth and social position between the inhabitants of Mecca widened. The difference was even greater when compared with the people of the desert.
The control of this Quraysh aristocracy over weaker groups also became harsher, including its control over small Meccan merchants.
These smaller traders could not compete with the great owners of commercial caravans. To take part in caravan journeys, they often had to borrow money at interest.
The interest charged could be extremely high—sometimes as much as one hundred percent.

The same kind of exploitation affected members of the desert tribes. They borrowed money at heavy rates of interest either to buy provisions before the seasonal markets or to earn a living through trade.
Moneylenders were also strict when demanding repayment of both the original loan and the interest. They gave debtors little time to recover financially.
A common saying of the period was that when a debt came due, the creditor would tell the debtor:
Usury brought large profits to the Quraysh aristocracy while bringing material hardship to weaker groups in towns, settled communities and the desert alike.
Their hardship was made worse by the taxes and charges imposed by the commercial aristocracy.
Small Arab traders who had no alliance with Quraysh had to pay them. Foreign merchants arriving in Mecca also had to pay them. So did caravans traveling from Syria to Yemen or from Yemen to Syria.
Among these charges was the tithe imposed on Byzantine merchants entering Mecca.
At the same time, the caravans belonging to this aristocracy had to make payments to the chiefs of the tribes whose territories they crossed, in return for protection along the route.
All these taxes, tolls and payments raised the cost of transported goods.

The burden eventually fell on consumers, agricultural producers, craftsmen and small traders. They had to pay higher prices for imported goods while receiving lower prices for the local products from which they earned their living.

Meanwhile, the caravans of Mecca’s financial and commercial aristocracy grew until some contained thousands of camels, while financial and commercial power became increasingly concentrated in their hands.
Once again, then, we can see how the trade of Quraysh and the activities of its moneylenders accelerated the breakdown already taking place within the tribal society of late pre-Islamic Arabia.
We should add that usury was not limited to the Quraysh aristocracy of Mecca.
There were moneylenders in Yathrib, al-Ṭāʾif, Yemen and other parts of the Arabian Peninsula who lived comfortably from interest without having to work for it.
Third — The Organization of Commercial Relations
The scale of the commercial activity carried out by the wealthy leaders of Quraysh required forms of trade organization that were highly developed by the standards of pre-Islamic Arabia.
Quraysh acted as commercial middlemen, traded with foreign countries, and operated in markets throughout Arabia.
These arrangements were clearly designed above all to benefit the upper group of Quraysh merchants and the people who dealt with them abroad, whether foreign governments or merchant groups.
Some of these arrangements concerned internal markets. Others concerned trade with foreign countries.
One important internal measure was the organization of seasonal markets, especially during the sacred months.
The timing of these markets was arranged so that trade could take place in peace and security during the months in which fighting was traditionally forbidden.
The pilgrimage season was one of the greatest sources of profit for Quraysh.
Quraysh sold goods to the Bedouins arriving from the desert and to the inhabitants of villages far from Mecca. In return, they bought the goods and raw materials these visitors brought with them.
Quraysh’s caravans then carried the surplus of what they had bought to foreign markets in Syria and Iraq.
There they purchased the goods and materials needed by the people of the Hijaz and by the Bedouins of the desert.

These internal arrangements also took other forms. Markets were protected through measures such as mukūs, fees collected from people selling goods there, and through taxes on sales profits. This kind of tax went back to the pre-Islamic period. The government of Qatabān originally collected one tenth of the profit made from buying or selling, but the tax was later extended until it was taken from profits of every kind. The same thing happened with other taxes: they went beyond what was needed for basic regulation and became a heavy burden on consumers, local producers, and small traders.

There were also rules governing many kinds of transactions, including leases, debts, pledges, and agricultural partnerships. Others dealt with property and housing, rights to use grazing land and the waters of rivers and springs, systems of weights, measures, and standards, and the handling of trusts, deposits, and written financial documents. Local alliances can also be included here, such as the alliance of Banū ʿAbd Manāf known as the Pact of the Perfumed Ones, and the alliances of Banū ʿAbd al-Dār.

The arrangements governing trade with the outside world seem to have been more highly developed. Their methods were more advanced, and they also helped improve commercial services, expand Arab trade, and push the social changes already under way toward new practical possibilities.

These arrangements can be seen in the kinds of relationships through which the Quraysh aristocracy pursued its commercial and economic interests with countries beyond Arabia. The remarkable success of the Meccan aristocracy as commercial middlemen between Arabia and many different countries—even countries at war with one another, such as Persia and Byzantium—could not have happened by accident. It would have been impossible if trade had simply been left to informal contacts and improvised dealings. Some fairly advanced form of organization, by the standards of the time, must have stood behind it.

It seems clear that long experience and wide foreign contacts gave the Quraysh aristocracy two important advantages. They understood the political struggle between Persia and Byzantium in considerable detail, and they had a keen sense of exactly where they had to position themselves between the two rival powers if they wanted to preserve their commercial interests with both.
This is why modern researchers have generally concluded that the people of Mecca adopted a neutral position between the Sasanians and the Byzantines, and that this neutrality served their interests.
Reports of their good relations with both the Romans and the Persians also suggest that these relationships were formally organized. It cannot have been a matter of chance, for example, that:

“The caravans travelling from Arabia to Syria would stop at particular markets assigned to them by the Roman government, so that it could collect the taxes imposed on ‘exports’ and keep watch over foreigners entering its territories. When these caravans first entered Roman territory, they stopped at Ayla, today known as Aqaba. From there they travelled to Gaza, where they came into contact with Mediterranean merchants. Some traders then continued from Gaza to Buṣrā.”

Arrangements this specific must have resulted from “official” agreements between the owners of these caravans, or representatives of the Quraysh leadership acting on their behalf, and the Roman government or its representatives in Syria and Palestine.

The motive behind such agreements was probably not limited to the desire for mutual commercial benefit. As the passage just quoted suggests, the Roman, or Byzantine, government also wanted to monitor the movements of Arab merchants in the territories it controlled near the Arabian Peninsula. This concern may have come from Byzantine doubts about whether the Meccan leadership was truly neutral in the political struggle between Byzantium and the Sasanians.

O’Leary supports this possibility. He does not rule out the idea that some of the Roman merchants living in Mecca—and the traditional historians tell us that some Roman traders did live there—may have spied on the Arabs for the Byzantines, reporting on Arab relations with Persia and on Persian contacts with the people of the peninsula.

In any case, there is little doubt that commercial relations between the Quraysh aristocracy and the Byzantines were governed by agreements with certain conditions and limits. The same was true of its relations with Persia and Abyssinia.

One well-known report says that Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf concluded a treaty with the Roman Empire, that ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAbd Manāf concluded a commercial treaty with the Negus of Abyssinia, and that Nawfal and al-Muṭṭalib, the sons of ʿAbd Manāf, made an alliance with Persia.

The traditional historians also preserve a number of accounts of the Quraysh īlāf mentioned in the Qurʾān. Their most common explanation is that Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf established the īlāf and was the first to introduce it:

“He obtained guarantees of protection (ʿiṣam) from the kings of Syria, and so they traded in safety. Then his brother ʿAbd Shams obtained guarantees for them—that is, for Quraysh—from the ruler of Abyssinia, where he himself traded. Al-Muṭṭalib ibn ʿAbd Manāf obtained guarantees for them from the kings of Yemen. And Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Manāf obtained guarantees for them from the kings of Iraq. They thus established the two journeys: in winter to Yemen, Abyssinia, and Iraq, and in summer to Syria.”
Almost all historians accept this explanation.
